replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is a single token — but the AI has *no idea* what it means until it looks at the words around it.

That's not a bug. It's the whole system.

**Tokenization** is step one. When you type a prompt, the model doesn't see letters or words — it breaks your text into chunks called *tokens*, then converts each one to a number.

A token is roughly a word or word-piece. "Running" might split into "run" + "ning." Punctuation gets its own token.

GPT-4's tokenizer knows about 100,000 different tokens.

[EX]Type "Hello, world!" and the model sees something like three tokens: "Hello", ",", " world!" — each mapped to a number. Those numbers are what actually travel through the system.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization turns your text into a sequence of numbers — that's the only form an LLM can work with.[/KEY]

[Q]
What does a language model actually receive when you type a prompt?
A) The exact letters and spaces you typed, preserved as text
B) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of your text
C) A lookup of your words in a dictionary database
ANS: B
[/Q]

Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is always the same token — whether you're talking about a riverbank or a savings account.

The model doesn't know which meaning you intend just from the word itself. Something else has to sort that out.

That "something else" is the first big idea: **tokenization**.

When you hit send, your prompt doesn't travel as words. It gets sliced into *tokens* — chunks that are roughly syllables or short words — and each token gets converted to a number.

[EX]"unbelievable" might become three tokens: "un" / "believ" / "able." A single emoji can be one token. A rare word might get split into many.[/EX]

B) Because neural networks do math on numbers, not on text
C) To compress the prompt and save memory

[/Q]

A token is roughly a word or word-chunk. "Unbelievable" might split into "un," "believ," and "able." GPT-4's tokenizer knows about 100,000 different tokens — and every single one gets converted to a number before the model touches it.

[KEY]Text becomes numbers (tokens) before an LLM can process it at all.[/KEY]

[EX]Type "Hello world" and the tokenizer might split it into ["Hello", " world"] — two tokens, two numbers, ready for the model.[/EX]

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually output when you type a sentence?
A) A dictionary definition of each word, looked up from a database
B) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of the text
C) A direct recording of the sentence's meaning and intent
ANS: B
